context_blurb:
A uranium fuel pellet about a centimetre across holds about as much energy as a ton of coal. That energy lies in the nucleus, an atom's tiny core: fission frees it by splitting a heavy nucleus, fusion by joining light ones.

Gravity is the feeblest of the four fundamental forces: between two protons, the electric push outdoes it a trillion trillion trillion times. Gravity still rules the Moon's path, because mass only attracts: the pull of every atom in Earth and the Moon adds up, while each body's plus and minus charges almost exactly cancel.

The strong force, felt by protons and neutrons alike, holds a nucleus together, pulling about a hundred times harder than its protons push each other apart. But it fades to almost nothing beyond two and a half trillionths of a millimetre, so each particle grips only the particles right next to it. Electrons do not feel it at all.

Albert Einstein's E = mc² says mass can turn into energy, a tiny mass into an enormous amount: one gram into about 90 trillion joules. A helium nucleus holds a little less mass than its two protons and two neutrons weighed apart: the mass defect. When the particles join, energy leaves them and carries a sliver of their mass away, so pulling the nucleus apart means putting that energy back.

Late in 1938, testing neutron-struck uranium in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann kept turning up barium. Hahn wrote to Lise Meitner, his partner in research for some thirty years, who had escaped Nazi Germany that July, and over Christmas in Sweden she worked it out with her nephew Otto Frisch. Barium's nucleus holds 56 protons, little more than half of uranium's 92, so the uranium nucleus had not been chipped or built up: it had split into two middle-sized nuclei. Frisch named it fission, after a cell dividing.

In Copenhagen the next January, Frisch tried to sink the idea. He coated a counting chamber inside with uranium, placed a neutron source nearby, and set the counter to ignore pulses as small as those from uranium's own alpha particles. Big pulses came. Splitting needs neutrons, so big pulses still arriving with the source taken away would have meant something else was making them, but in hours of check runs he saw none. Hahn alone won the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; Meitner was left out.

Each split of a uranium-235 nucleus, set off when it captures a neutron, throws out two or three new neutrons for other uranium-235 nuclei to capture in turn: a chain reaction. The two flying pieces split nothing; their speed becomes heat. Water round the fuel carries the heat away to make steam for a turbine, in the most common designs by heating a separate loop. Control rods of boron or cadmium soak up neutrons before those can split more nuclei, so rods pushed in slow the reaction and rods lowered fully stop it. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, and it makes splits likelier, not rarer.

Fusion joins light nuclei, such as deuterium and tritium, hydrogen's two heavy forms, into helium. Every nucleus is positively charged, so two nuclei push each other away, and only nuclei moving very fast, which means very hot, come close enough for the short-reaching strong force to take hold. So the fuel is heated past 100 million degrees Celsius into plasma, bare nuclei and free electrons; nothing burns.

In California in December 2022, the National Ignition Facility fired lasers into a tiny gold can holding a frozen fuel pellet. The fusion gave out 3.15 megajoules (millions of joules) against 2.05 of laser light, the first time a pellet had given out more energy than the lasers put in: ignition. But its lasers drew about 300 megajoules from the grid, and no fusion machine yet makes more electricity than it uses.

A nuclear plant runs in any weather and, over its life, releases about as little carbon dioxide per unit of electricity as wind. Its used fuel, solid pellets in metal rods, cools for years in water pools, then goes into steel-and-concrete casks, which give off a little radiation, within limits, and have been shipped thousands of times without any radioactive material escaping. The hard part is time: used fuel stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years and must be kept away from people all that while. Finland has built the world's first deep underground store; the United States still has no permanent one.
